paper.note: Covering report only. Appendix 1 (prudential indicators) is referenced at 4.3 but is not included in this PDF — nothing said in the note about authorised limit, operational boundary or maturity-band limits.

facts.value: £575m total (General Fund £509m, HRA £66m); £541m borrowing CFR after £34m of PFI and lease liabilities
facts.note: Table 1 foots exactly at both steps. 2025-26 is indicative pending the Statement of Accounts; the footnote flags a presentational difference against Note 38 of the draft accounts on the PFI liability that does not affect borrowing levels.

facts.value: £234m — PWLB £212m at 3.75% over 16.1 years, LOBO £7m at 4.65% over 17.7 years, bank fixed-term £15m at 4.68% over 20.4 years
facts.note: Sums to £234m exactly (212 + 7 + 15). Only £5m matured in year and a single £10m one-year PWLB loan was taken as replacement (4.14).

Their own figure at 4.10. Balance-sheet identity: £541m borrowing CFR − £234m external = £307m. Or £575m total CFR − £234m external − £34m other debt = £307m. Both exact. More of the capital programme is funded from cash than from loans.

Ties to Table 3's £212m to the £m as printed. Weighted rate on our file 3.89% against their Table 3 rate of 3.75% — a 14bp gap, likely effective-interest accounting on their side. Their WAM of 16.1 years is quoted verbatim; not directly testable without their EIR-weighted balances.

facts.value: net DISCOUNT £19,278,449 (9.1% of principal); indicative settlement £191,481,685; 39 of 51 loans below par
facts.note: DMO premature repayment curve, notice 314/26 PM, 14 August 2026. Live balance £210,760,134 across the 51 loans. Largest single discount PW499702 (ANNUITY 2042, 3.18% coupon, £46.95m balance, −£5.08m). INDICATIVE ONLY — only the DMO can quote.

facts.value: the capital financing budget underspent by £3.1m — £2.4m purely because loans were not taken; £0.7m from a lower MRP charge
facts.note: Budget £20.9m against £17.8m expenditure. Both components (£0.7m + £2.4m = £3.1m) foot exactly.

facts.value: £84m — money market funds £73m at 3.78%, equity income funds £5m at 7.43%, property funds £4m at 5.98%, banks £2m at 2.59%
facts.note: Sums to £84m exactly. £10m of strategic pooled funds (equity + property) generated £0.51m of income in 2025-26 (4.21). Balances ranged £57m–£174m across the year (4.17). IFRS 9 statutory override extended to March 2029 (4.23).

facts.value: £7m at 4.65%; lender's next option date 25 May 2027
facts.note: A diary item rather than a live decision, unlike most LOBO books we hold.

facts.value: their 31 March 2026 one-year certainty rate of 5.04% and 25-year of 6.29% match our published series exactly
of the LOBO calls we have logged across councils in recent months, every one has been refused; Oldham published being offered 6.70% and 7.67%, Wolverhampton 6.19%, 6.21% and 6.26%
facts.note: NOT from Cheshire West's own paper — cited as sector context. Legitimate to include because their 25 May 2027 option date is far enough out that lenders will decide with a fresh curve, and the pattern is one no single council can see.

summary.text:
£307m of internal borrowing against £234m of external. Cheshire West has funded more of its capital programme from its own cash than from loans, says so plainly at 4.10, and the saving is visible: a £3.1m underspend on the capital financing budget, £2.4m of it purely because the loans were not taken. The only borrowing all year was a single £10m one-year PWLB loan replacing £5m that matured.

The balance sheet ties exactly — CFR £575m less £34m of PFI and leases is the £541m borrowing CFR, less £234m of external borrowing is the £307m they state at 4.10. Our own PWLB file (51 loans, £212.3m at 31 March) ties to their Table 3 £212m to the £m; the weighted rate differs by 14bp (our 3.89% vs their 3.75%), most likely effective-interest accounting.

The investment side has an unusual shape for a council this size: £73m of £84m in money market funds at 3.78%, but £5m of equity income funds returning 7.43% and £4m of property funds 5.98%. Balances swung from £57m to £174m across the year — the trough of that range, not the average, is what sets when internal borrowing must become external at a £307m under-borrowed position.

The £7m LOBO with a next option date of 25 May 2027 is a diary item rather than a live decision. Appendix 1 (prudential indicators) is referenced but not attached to this PDF, so nothing said about limits.

Contact is published in the report — Debbie Hall, Director of Finance, with a direct number and address.

PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator
officer.body:
Hi Debbie,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the annual report that went to Audit and Governance on 21 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first. Every table in your report foots against the others, which is rarer than it should be: CFR of £575m is General Fund £509m plus HRA £66m; less £34m of PFI and lease liabilities gives the £541m borrowing CFR; less £234m of external borrowing gives the £307m of internal borrowing you state at 4.10. Table 3 sums to £234m and Table 4 to £84m. Our own PWLB file holds 51 loans at £212.3m as at 31 March against your Table 3 £212m, so we're looking at the same book. One small discrepancy to flag rather than gloss: our weighted rate on those 51 loans comes out at 3.89% against your 3.75%, a 14 basis point gap. Effective-interest accounting on your side is the most likely explanation and both figures can be right on their own basis, but worth surfacing.

The £307m is the story and you have already told it well — cash balances funding capital instead of loans, one £10m one-year PWLB loan taken all year to replace £5m that matured, and a £3.1m underspend on the capital financing budget of which £2.4m is purely borrowing not taken. That is a large, deliberate and demonstrably cheaper position, and we have no suggestion to make about it.

Where we might be useful is the bit underneath it. Your investment balances ranged from £57m to £174m during the year — a £117m swing — while the under-borrowed position sat at £307m. That combination means the question "when does internal borrowing have to become external" is not answered by the average balance but by the trough, and the trough is a cashflow question rather than a strategy one. The liability benchmark is the indicator built for exactly that, and it is the one CIPFA has been pushing hardest on in its forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates. We publish live curves behind it so the crossing point moves with the market rather than being recalculated annually.

For the market itself: one-year PWLB certainty closed at 4.95% yesterday afternoon on notice 314/26, five-year at 5.34% and ten-year at 5.83%, against your existing PWLB book at 3.75%. July's sector lending was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%, which is thin — worth knowing before you need to be in it rather than after. That breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

Two smaller observations. Your investment mix is unusual for a council your size and in a good way: £73m of the £84m sits in money market funds at 3.78%, but the £5m of equity income funds returned 7.43% and the £4m of property funds 5.98% — £10m of strategic pooled funds producing £0.51m between them. Most councils we read either hold none of this or hold a single CCLA position; two different fund types actually earning their keep is worth noticing, particularly with the IFRS 9 override now running to March 2029.

And on the borrowing side, your PWLB book prices about £19.3m below par on the DMO's premature repayment curve today, with 39 of the 51 loans in discount. Nothing follows from that: we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, only the DMO can quote, and whether anything would be worth doing turns on replacement cost we do not model. Yours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

Your £7m LOBO with a next option date of 25 May 2027 is far enough out to be a diary item. For context, of the LOBO calls we have picked up across councils in recent months every single one was refused — Oldham published being offered 6.70% and 7.67%, Wolverhampton 6.19%, 6.21% and 6.26%. Lenders are testing options now that PWLB rates have risen to meet them, so May 2027 is more likely to be tested than not. That is a cross-council picture no single council can see from its own papers.

On training, four fit Cheshire West. Liability Benchmark: using it in practice and Cash-flow forecasting & daily cash go to the £307m and the £117m swing. Pooled funds (CCLA, multi-asset) for the equity income and property holdings. And PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.
